3. Deep Dive: Preparing Forest Plot Inputs

Part3-deep-dive-forest-plot-inputs.Rmd
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(PMXForest)
  library(dplyr)
})

set.seed(865765)

Introduction

getForestDFSCM() takes four inputs. The Quick start and the Walkthrough build all four with the convenience functions, which is the right way to work. This vignette is for the times that is not enough: when you need to know what a convenience function decided on your behalf, override one step of it, or build an input the wrappers do not cover.

So the table below reads in both directions. Left to right, it is what each input is and which one call produces it. Right to left, it is what that call does underneath — the function to reach for when you want to take over.

Input What it is One call What that call does underneath
dfCovs one row per Forest plot row, inactive cells at -99 setupDfCovs() getCovStats() picks the values to plot, then createInputForestData() lays them out as rows
functionList a list of one or more parameter functions: typical values from thetas and covariates createParamFunction() nmParsePK() parses $PK, nmCovRef() finds a reference for each covariate, then the tree is emitted as R source
dfRefRow the reference subject the other rows are expressed relative to setupDfRefRow() refResolve() resolves one reference per covariate (refValues() from the data, the $PK for "model"), shaped into a single row matching dfCovs
dfParameters parameter uncertainty samples getSamples() this is the primitive — it reads the .cov, bootstrap or SIR file directly
covExpressionsList which subjects each empirical row summarises setupCovExpressionsList() applies the same level and quantile rules as getCovStats(), but implements them separately rather than calling it, because the two return different shapes

The empirical entry point getForestDFemp() takes a covExpressionsList in place of dfCovs; that is covered in Section 7.

There is a third way to read the table, and it matters more than either. A convenience function encodes one reasonable answer to “what should this input look like?” — the observed percentiles, one row per level, the reference the control stream implies. When that answer does not fit the question you are asking, the fix is usually not to abandon the function and build the input by hand. It is to take what the function produced and change the part that is wrong, in script rather than by retyping.

That keeps the provenance: what came from the data or the model is still derived, the deviation is a visible line of code that a reviewer can see and question, and re-running after the model or the data changes reproduces both the derivation and the deviation. Sections 1 and 2 each end with a worked example.

Two of those rows are worth pausing on. setupDfCovs() is a genuine composition — you can call getCovStats() and createInputForestData() yourself and get the same object, which Section 1 does step by step. setupCovExpressionsList() is not: it duplicates the logic. If you change how one of them chooses levels or quantiles, the other does not follow.

The data throughout is the PK data file used in the Walkthrough, read as it comes rather than filtered through the model’s IGNORE statements, and the model is the run7 control stream bundled with the package.

dataFile <- system.file("extdata", "SimVal/DAT-1-MI-PMX-2.csv", package = "PMXForest")
modFile <- system.file("extdata", "SimVal/run7.mod", package = "PMXForest")
dfData <- read.csv(dataFile)

1. Covariate values: dfCovs

getCovStats()

getCovStats() returns a named list, one element per covariate. The element type depends on the number of unique values:

  • continuous (more than minLevels unique values) — a two-element numeric vector of quantiles, by default the 5th and 95th percentiles;
  • binary — the two levels, sorted alphanumerically;
  • multi-level categorical — a nested list of one-hot vectors. The reference level (the lowest level, or the one named in catRef) is the all-zero row.
covStats <- getCovStats(
  data       = dfData,
  covariates = c("WT", "AGE", "SEX", "GENO"),
  idVar      = "ID"
)
covStats
#> $WT
#>    5%   95% 
#>  58.5 126.0 
#> 
#> $AGE
#>  5% 95% 
#>  22  65 
#> 
#> $SEX
#> [1] 1 2
#> 
#> $GENO
#> $GENO$GENO_2
#> [1] 0 1 0 0
#> 
#> $GENO$GENO_3
#> [1] 0 0 1 0
#> 
#> $GENO$GENO_4
#> [1] 0 0 0 1

Statistics are computed on the first record per idVar, so subjects with dense sampling do not pull the quantiles.

nrow(dfData) # all records
#> [1] 69016
nrow(distinct(dfData, ID)) # subjects
#> [1] 964

minLevels (default 10) is the threshold between categorical and continuous. A covariate coded with a small number of distinct numeric values — a dose level, an ordinal score — is treated as categorical unless minLevels is lowered.

## GENO has 4 levels: categorical by default
getCovStats(dfData, "GENO", idVar = "ID")
#> $GENO
#> $GENO$GENO_2
#> [1] 0 1 0 0
#> 
#> $GENO$GENO_3
#> [1] 0 0 1 0
#> 
#> $GENO$GENO_4
#> [1] 0 0 0 1

## Force GENO to be treated as continuous
getCovStats(dfData, "GENO", idVar = "ID", minLevels = 3)
#> $GENO
#>  5% 95% 
#>   2   4

probs sets the quantiles for continuous covariates; nsig sets the rounding.

getCovStats(dfData, "CRCL", idVar = "ID", probs = c(0.1, 0.9), nsig = 4)
#> $CRCL
#>    10%    90% 
#>  83.66 150.00

catRef and sep

By default the lowest level of a multi-level categorical is the reference (the all-zero row) and the one-hot columns are named <covariate>_<level>. catRef overrides the reference level per covariate; sep changes the separator. (catRef replaces refLevels, which still works but is deprecated.)

## GENO reference is level 1 by default -> columns GENO_2, GENO_3, GENO_4
getCovStats(dfData, "GENO", idVar = "ID")
#> $GENO
#> $GENO$GENO_2
#> [1] 0 1 0 0
#> 
#> $GENO$GENO_3
#> [1] 0 0 1 0
#> 
#> $GENO$GENO_4
#> [1] 0 0 0 1

## Make level 2 the reference -> columns GENO_1, GENO_3, GENO_4
getCovStats(dfData, "GENO", idVar = "ID", catRef = list(GENO = 2))
#> $GENO
#> $GENO$GENO_1
#> [1] 1 0 0 0
#> 
#> $GENO$GENO_3
#> [1] 0 0 1 0
#> 
#> $GENO$GENO_4
#> [1] 0 0 0 1

Use catRef when the model’s reference category is not the lowest level — otherwise the one-hot columns will not line up with the model’s coefficients. The "_" separator matches NONMEM FREM data sets and PMXFrem::createFREMModel(); change it only if you have a reason to.

Binary levels are returned in alphanumeric order (c(0, 1)), not order of appearance in the data. Forest plot row order is therefore reproducible across data sets.

createInputForestData()

createInputForestData() turns a covariate list into the row structure. It is what you call directly when the covariate values are known literals rather than derived from data.

dfCovsManual <- createInputForestData(
  list(
    "WT"   = c(60, 100),
    "SEX"  = c(1, 2),
    "GENO" = list("GENO_2" = c(0, 1, 0), "GENO_3" = c(0, 0, 1), "GENO_4" = c(0, 0, 0))
  ),
  iMiss = -99
)
dfCovsManual
#>    WT SEX GENO_2 GENO_3 GENO_4 COVARIATEGROUPS
#> 1  60 -99    -99    -99    -99              WT
#> 2 100 -99    -99    -99    -99              WT
#> 3 -99   1    -99    -99    -99             SEX
#> 4 -99   2    -99    -99    -99             SEX
#> 5 -99 -99      0      0      0            GENO
#> 6 -99 -99      1      0      0            GENO
#> 7 -99 -99      0      1      0            GENO

The COVARIATEGROUPS column records which covariate each row belongs to; getForestDFSCM() uses it to group and space the rows on the y-axis, and drops it before calling the parameter function.

A getCovStats() result can be passed straight in:

createInputForestData(covStats, iMiss = -99)
#>       WT AGE SEX GENO_2 GENO_3 GENO_4 COVARIATEGROUPS
#> 1   58.5 -99 -99    -99    -99    -99              WT
#> 2  126.0 -99 -99    -99    -99    -99              WT
#> 3  -99.0  22 -99    -99    -99    -99             AGE
#> 4  -99.0  65 -99    -99    -99    -99             AGE
#> 5  -99.0 -99   1    -99    -99    -99             SEX
#> 6  -99.0 -99   2    -99    -99    -99             SEX
#> 7  -99.0 -99 -99      0      0      0            GENO
#> 8  -99.0 -99 -99      1      0      0            GENO
#> 9  -99.0 -99 -99      0      1      0            GENO
#> 10 -99.0 -99 -99      0      0      1            GENO

setupDfCovs()

setupDfCovs() runs getCovStats() and createInputForestData() together and adds control over how inactive cells are filled.

covariates <- c("WT", "AGE", "CRCL", "SEX", "NCIL", "GENO")

dfCovs <- setupDfCovs(data = dfData, covariates = covariates, idVar = "ID")
dfCovs
#>       WT AGE  CRCL SEX NCIL GENO_2 GENO_3 GENO_4 COVARIATEGROUPS
#> 1   58.5 -99 -99.0 -99  -99    -99    -99    -99              WT
#> 2  126.0 -99 -99.0 -99  -99    -99    -99    -99              WT
#> 3  -99.0  22 -99.0 -99  -99    -99    -99    -99             AGE
#> 4  -99.0  65 -99.0 -99  -99    -99    -99    -99             AGE
#> 5  -99.0 -99  74.9 -99  -99    -99    -99    -99            CRCL
#> 6  -99.0 -99 150.0 -99  -99    -99    -99    -99            CRCL
#> 7  -99.0 -99 -99.0   1  -99    -99    -99    -99             SEX
#> 8  -99.0 -99 -99.0   2  -99    -99    -99    -99             SEX
#> 9  -99.0 -99 -99.0 -99    0    -99    -99    -99            NCIL
#> 10 -99.0 -99 -99.0 -99    1    -99    -99    -99            NCIL
#> 11 -99.0 -99 -99.0 -99  -99      0      0      0            GENO
#> 12 -99.0 -99 -99.0 -99  -99      1      0      0            GENO
#> 13 -99.0 -99 -99.0 -99  -99      0      1      0            GENO
#> 14 -99.0 -99 -99.0 -99  -99      0      0      1            GENO

Covariates listed in conditionalCovs get their own rows, but on every other row they sit at their reference rather than at -99. This is for covariates on which the other covariates are conditioned, eg fed state (instead of fasted) or patients (instead of healthy volunteers).

setupDfCovs(
  data            = dfData,
  covariates      = c("WT", "AGE", "SEX"),
  conditionalCovs = "CRCL",
  idVar           = "ID"
)
#>      WT AGE SEX  CRCL COVARIATEGROUPS
#> 1  58.5 -99 -99 118.0              WT
#> 2 126.0 -99 -99 118.0              WT
#> 3 -99.0  22 -99 118.0             AGE
#> 4 -99.0  65 -99 118.0             AGE
#> 5 -99.0 -99   1 118.0             SEX
#> 6 -99.0 -99   2 118.0             SEX
#> 7 -99.0 -99 -99  74.9            CRCL
#> 8 -99.0 -99 -99 150.0            CRCL

On the WT, AGE, and SEX rows, CRCL holds its median instead of -99.

With useMissVal = FALSE, inactive primary covariates are also set to their reference, so the parameter function never sees -99.

setupDfCovs(
  data       = dfData,
  covariates = c("WT", "AGE", "SEX"),
  useMissVal = FALSE,
  idVar      = "ID"
)
#>      WT AGE SEX COVARIATEGROUPS
#> 1  58.5  47   1              WT
#> 2 126.0  47   1              WT
#> 3  85.4  22   1             AGE
#> 4  85.4  65   1             AGE
#> 5  85.4  47   1             SEX
#> 6  85.4  47   2             SEX

Adjusting what setupDfCovs() produced

setupDfCovs() gives one row per level and the 5th/95th percentiles of the observed data. Two things it will not do: use a value the study did not observe, and show a combination of covariates, since it varies one at a time.

Both are ordinary requirements — a label may specify weight bands rather than percentiles, and the clinical question is often “what about a light poor metaboliser?”, which no single-covariate row answers. Start from the generated structure and edit it.

dfCovsAdj <- setupDfCovs(dfData,
  covariates = c("WT", "GENO"),
  catRef = list(GENO = 2), sep = "", idVar = "ID"
)
dfCovsAdj
#>      WT GENO1 GENO3 GENO4 COVARIATEGROUPS
#> 1  58.5   -99   -99   -99              WT
#> 2 126.0   -99   -99   -99              WT
#> 3 -99.0     1     0     0            GENO
#> 4 -99.0     0     0     0            GENO
#> 5 -99.0     0     1     0            GENO
#> 6 -99.0     0     0     1            GENO

A combination row is built from any existing row, so it is guaranteed to have the right columns in the right order. Blank it to missVal, then set only the cells the row is about:

combo <- dfCovsAdj[1, ]
combo[setdiff(names(combo), "COVARIATEGROUPS")] <- -99
combo$WT <- 60
combo$GENO1 <- 0
combo$GENO3 <- 0
combo$GENO4 <- 1
combo$COVARIATEGROUPS <- "Combination"

dfCovsAdj <- rbind(dfCovsAdj, combo)
tail(dfCovsAdj, 2)
#>    WT GENO1 GENO3 GENO4 COVARIATEGROUPS
#> 6 -99     0     0     1            GENO
#> 7  60     0     0     1     Combination

Note that all three genotype columns are set, not just GENO4. A one-hot covariate is only inactive when every one of its columns holds missVal; leaving GENO1 and GENO3 at -99 while GENO4 is 1 is a contradiction the parameter function would resolve by falling back to the reference for the two it cannot read.

Row labels are supplied separately and are not regenerated, so extend them in the same step and keep the stopifnot() guard:

covnamesAdj <- c(
  paste0("WT ", dfCovsAdj$WT[1:2], " kg"),
  "2D6 UM", "2D6 EM", "2D6 IM", "2D6 PM",
  "60 kg, 2D6 PM"
)
stopifnot(length(covnamesAdj) == nrow(dfCovsAdj))

The same approach covers replacing a percentile with a protocol value (dfCovsAdj$WT[1:2] <- c(60, 100)) or dropping a row you do not want to show (dfCovsAdj[-3, ]). What it does not cover is a different shape of input — for that, createInputForestData() builds one from literal values directly, as above.

oneHotEncode()

getCovStats() produces one-hot vectors from a summary of the data. oneHotEncode() does the same job on a data frame: it adds <covariate><sep><level> dummy columns to whatever data frame you give it. This is what the oneHot argument of getForestDFSCM() and getForestDFemp() calls internally, and it follows the same convention as NONMEM FREM data sets.

raw <- data.frame(
  ID   = 1:6,
  GENO = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 2, -99),
  RACE = c(1, 1, 2, 3, 2, 1)
)

## Lowest level as reference; missing rows kept as missVal
oneHotEncode(raw, spec = c("GENO", "RACE"))
#>   ID GENO RACE GENO_2 GENO_3 GENO_4 RACE_2 RACE_3
#> 1  1    1    1      0      0      0      0      0
#> 2  2    2    1      1      0      0      0      0
#> 3  3    3    2      0      1      0      1      0
#> 4  4    4    3      0      0      1      0      1
#> 5  5    2    2      1      0      0      1      0
#> 6  6  -99    1    -99    -99    -99      0      0

The reference level is set the same way as in getCovStats():

oneHotEncode(raw, spec = list(GENO = list(ref = 2)), dropOriginal = TRUE)
#>   ID RACE GENO_1 GENO_3 GENO_4
#> 1  1    1      1      0      0
#> 2  2    1      0      0      0
#> 3  3    2      0      1      0
#> 4  4    3      0      0      1
#> 5  5    2      0      0      0
#> 6  6    1    -99    -99    -99
Argument Effect
includeReference also create a dummy column for the reference level
imputeMissing TRUE sets missing rows to 0 (the reference); FALSE (default) keeps missVal
dropOriginal remove the raw column after encoding
sep separator in the new column names (default "_")

oneHotEncode() is idempotent: a dummy column that already exists and agrees with the requested encoding is left untouched; one that disagrees raises an error. This makes it safe to run on data that already carries FREM dummy columns.

2. The parameter function: createParamFunction

The parameter function turns a vector of thetas and one row of covariate values into the parameters to plot. Writing it by hand duplicates code that already exists in the control stream, and it is the easiest place in the whole workflow to introduce a silent error.

2.1 What a parameter function must do

Before generating one, it is worth knowing what is being generated — both to read the output critically and to write one yourself when the generator cannot (Section 2.3).

The contract is:

function(thetas, df, ...) {
  # ... rebuild the model's typical values from thetas and df ...
  list(<quantity 1>, <quantity 2>, ...)
}
  • thetas is a numeric vector, in the order the THETAs appear in the model.
  • df is a one-row data frame of covariate values — one Forest plot row. Because it is one row, if (df$WT != -99) is a scalar condition, which is what makes the guards below legal.
  • ... absorbs anything else getForestDFSCM() passes through, such as the extra arguments the time-to-event vignette uses.
  • The return value is a list of the quantities to plot.

Nothing about those quantities is fixed. The function decides what to compute and in what order; getForestDFSCM() reads the list by position and takes the names from functionListName, which you supply alongside it. So

functionList     = list(myFunction)
functionListName = c("CL", "Frel", "AUC", "V")

names the first returned element CL, the second Frel, and so on — the names in the plot come from functionListName, not from the function. A list that is itself named is fine and often clearer to read, but the names are ignored, and a mismatch in order between the two silently mislabels every panel. Keep the return and functionListName next to each other for that reason.

functionList is a list because it may hold more than one function. Each is evaluated for every row and every parameter vector, and their results are concatenated in order, so functionListName names the returns of all of them end to end:

functionList     = list(pkFunction, exposureFunction)
functionListName = c("CL", "V", "AUC", "Cmax")   # 2 from the first, 2 from the second

Splitting the work up this way is worth it when one part is cheap and another is not — a closed-form PK function alongside one that runs a simulation — or when the quantities come from genuinely different models. The time-to-event vignette uses two functions for a related reason: a hazard ratio and a cumulative distribution need different x-axis scales, so they are computed and plotted separately.

Two defensive checks apply to every covariate the function reads:

  • any(names(df) == "WT") — the column may be absent entirely.
  • df$WT != -99 — the cell may hold the missing-value indicator, which dfCovs uses for every covariate that is inactive on that row.

The second is the one that surprises people. It is needed even when the original NONMEM data has no missing covariate values at all, because -99 here does not mean “missing in the data” — it means “this row is not about this covariate”. A dfCovs row that varies WT carries -99 in SEX, FOOD and the genotype columns, and a function that reads df$SEX without the guard will compute a covariate effect for a row that was never meant to have one.

Written out for a single covariate, the shape is:

FRELSEX <- 1
if (any(names(df) == "SEX") && df$SEX != -99 && df$SEX == 2) {
  FRELSEX <- 1 + thetas[14]
}

Note the ordering: the column check comes first, so df$SEX is only evaluated once it is known to exist. Note also df[["SEX"]] would be safer still — $ partial-matches on a data frame, so a data set carrying SEXF but not SEX would silently supply the wrong column. The generated function uses the bracket form for exactly this reason.

A full hand-written function for run7, kept deliberately as a comparison against the generated one, is in inst/validation/compare-paramFunction.R in the installed package.

2.2 Generating one

createParamFunction() translates the $PK block into R source text for you to read, check and edit. Nothing is evaluated on your behalf.

gen <- createParamFunction(
  modFile,
  parameters = c("CL", "FREL", "V"),
  covRef     = list(GENO1 = 0, GENO3 = 0),
  quiet      = TRUE
)
cat(head(gen$code, 24), sep = "\n")
#> ## Generated by PMXForest::createParamFunction() from run7.mod.
#> ## Typical values: every ETA() in $PK has been set to 0.
#> ## Review this against the control stream before use.
#> 
#> paramFunction <- function(thetas, df, ...) {
#> 
#>   ## ---- Covariate references, taken from run7.mod --------------------------------------
#>   ## SEX    reference level of the ";  Most common" branch  [run7.mod:18]
#>   SEX   <- if (!is.null(df[["SEX"]]) && df[["SEX"]] != -99) df[["SEX"]] else 1
#>   ## GENO4  reference level of the ";  Most common" branch  [run7.mod:24]
#>   GENO4 <- if (!is.null(df[["GENO4"]]) && df[["GENO4"]] != -99) df[["GENO4"]] else 0
#>   ## FORM   reference level of the ";  Most common" branch  [run7.mod:30]
#>   FORM  <- if (!is.null(df[["FORM"]]) && df[["FORM"]] != -99) df[["FORM"]] else 1
#>   ## FOOD   reference level of the ";  Most common" branch  [run7.mod:40]
#>   FOOD  <- if (!is.null(df[["FOOD"]]) && df[["FOOD"]] != -99) df[["FOOD"]] else 1
#>   ## WT     normalisation constant in (WT / 75)  [run7.mod:53]
#>   WT    <- if (!is.null(df[["WT"]]) && df[["WT"]] != -99) df[["WT"]] else 75
#>   ## GENO1  supplied through covRef
#>   GENO1 <- if (!is.null(df[["GENO1"]]) && df[["GENO1"]] != -99) df[["GENO1"]] else 0
#>   ## GENO3  supplied through covRef
#>   GENO3 <- if (!is.null(df[["GENO3"]]) && df[["GENO3"]] != -99) df[["GENO3"]] else 0
#> 
#>   ## ---- $PK, transliterated ---------------------------------------------------
#>   if (SEX == 1) FRELSEX <- 1

The final estimates are what the function will be evaluated with, here and in getForestDFSCM():

ext <- getExt(system.file("extdata", "SimVal/run7.ext", package = "PMXForest"))
thetas <- as.numeric(ext[ext$ITERATION == -1000000000, 2:15])

Two things to notice.

Every ETA(n) is set to 0, so the function returns typical values — what a Forest plot needs.

All missing-covariate handling is hoisted into one preamble, annotated with where each reference came from, after which the $PK algebra below is a plain transliteration you can diff line by line against the control stream. The references are read out of the control stream itself, by four rules in decreasing order of confidence:

Rule Source
1 explicit handling, IF(WT.EQ.-99) WT = 75
2a the branch PsN’s scm marks ; Most common
2b the branch assigning the identity value (1 multiplicative, 0 additive)
3 the normalisation constant in (WT/75) or (AGE-50) 
gen$covRef$WT
#> $value
#> [1] 75
#> 
#> $line
#> [1] 53
#> 
#> $confident
#> [1] TRUE
#> 
#> $source
#> [1] "normalisation constant in (WT / 75)"
#> 
#> $inArithmetic
#> [1] TRUE

A weaker fifth rule proposes the level that no IF() tests and warns; confirm it through covRef, as above for GENO1 and GENO3. A covariate matching no rule at all is an error, not a guess.

2.3 When the generator refuses

The parser accepts assignments, IF constructs and closed-form arithmetic. It refuses anything it cannot translate faithfully, naming the file and line rather than guessing:

Refused Why
A(1) — a compartment amount needs an ODE solution, which no closed-form function can supply
DO, WHILE, CALL, GOTO, RETURN control flow with no expression equivalent
verbatim FORTRAN not NM-TRAN, so not parseable as such
EPS() / ERR() residual error has no place in a typical-value function
a symbol read before anything assigns it see below

That last one is worth explaining, because NONMEM accepts it and R will not. NM-TRAN’s abbreviated-code rules are explicit about what happens when a conditional assignment does not fire, and they distinguish two cases:

IF (WT.GT.0) TVK=THETA(1)*WT If the condition is false, the non-random variable TVK retains the value set with the previous data record.

IF (WT.GT.0) K=THETA(1)*WT*EXP(ETA(1)) If the condition is false, the value of the random variable K is set to zero.

So a variable without an ETA carries its value across records — a parameter function is evaluated one row at a time with no previous record to carry from, and cannot reproduce that. A variable with an ETA is zeroed instead, which a generated function cannot reproduce either, since it has no equivalent notion of a random variable once every ETA() has been set to 0.

createParamFunction() therefore refuses rather than quietly substituting a zero and being right only half the time. If you hit this, give the variable an unconditional value in $PK above the line that reads it.

A branch chain with no ELSE is accepted, because scm writes exhaustive ones — run7.mod itself sets FRELFORM from two one-line IFs covering FORM 0 and 1 — and no static check can tell an exhaustive chain from a non-exhaustive one. If no branch fires at run time the generated function stops with object not found, which is the honest outcome.

When the generator refuses, write the function by hand to the contract in Section 2.1. Two vignettes do exactly that, for models the generator cannot reach:

  • Time-to-event models — hazard and CDF functions, including passing extra arguments through ....
  • R-coded models — a model that never had a $PK block to parse.

2.4 Adjusting the generated function

The generator returns source text, which is the reason it returns text at all: a function you disagree with can be corrected without abandoning the translation that was right.

Section 2.3 noted one case where the generated function is faithful to the control stream and still not enough. run7’s $PK sets the sex effect with two one-line branches and no ELSE:

cat(grep("FRELSEX", gen$code, value = TRUE), sep = "\n")
#>   if (SEX == 1) FRELSEX <- 1
#>   if (SEX == 2) FRELSEX <- 1 + thetas[14]
#>   FRELCOV <- FRELFORM * FRELGENO4 * FRELSEX

That is exhaustive for the data the model was fitted to, where SEX is 1 or 2. It is not exhaustive in general, and NONMEM’s implicit carry-over between records hides the difference. In R there is nothing to carry over:

paramFunction <- eval(parse(text = paste(gen$code, collapse = "\n")))
paramFunction(thetas, df = data.frame(SEX = 3))
#> Error in paramFunction(thetas, df = data.frame(SEX = 3)): object 'FRELSEX' not found

The repair is one line, inserted where the branches begin — and inserted by matching on the text rather than by counting lines, so it still lands in the right place after the model is re-run and the source regenerated:

code <- gen$code
at <- grep("if (SEX == 1) FRELSEX <- 1", code, fixed = TRUE)
code <- append(code, "  FRELSEX <- 1  # default the scm branches leave implicit", after = at - 1)

paramFunctionFixed <- eval(parse(text = paste(code, collapse = "\n")))

The unmodelled level now resolves to the reference, and the modelled ones are untouched — which is the property to check after any edit of this kind:

vapply(1:3, function(s) paramFunctionFixed(thetas, data.frame(SEX = s))$FREL, numeric(1))
#> [1] 1.000000 0.861085 1.000000

Three habits make this safe rather than a fork of the model:

Edit the object, not a copy. gen$code is a character vector, so the change is sub(), grep() and append() in the script. Pasting the generated source into the file and hand-editing it there produces something that looks hand-written, cannot be regenerated, and will silently disagree with the model after the next run.

Match on content, not position. code[24] is correct until a covariate is added to $PK. grep(..., fixed = TRUE) on the line’s text still finds it, and length(at) == 1 is worth asserting if the pattern could match twice.

Say why, in the code. The inserted line carries a comment. When someone asks in six months why the Forest plot does not match the control stream exactly, the answer is in the script rather than in anyone’s memory.

If the edit grows past a few lines, that is a signal the model needs the correction rather than the plot — fix $PK and regenerate.

Secondary parameters are yours

AUC, Cmax and event probabilities are not derivable from $PK — the dose used for an AUC appears nowhere in the control stream, and anything through $ERROR or $DES needs an ODE solution. The emitted source carries a marked extension point for you to add them:

cat(grep("Secondary parameters", gen$code, value = TRUE))
#>   ## ---- Secondary parameters: add yours below ---------------------------------

You do not have to add them by editing the emitted text. secondary takes them as an argument, either as a line of R code or as the path to a whole .R file — an mrgsolve or deSolve simulation, say — which is inlined so the result stays self-contained. That is a topic in itself, and it has its own vignette: Secondary parameters.

Checking the translation: verifyParamFunction()

verifyParamFunction() evaluates the generated function over a NONMEM $TABLE file and compares the result with the values NONMEM itself wrote, which turns “do I trust this translation?” into a pass or a fail.

v <- verifyParamFunction(gen, tabFile = "xptab7", thetas = thetas)
v
#> PASS - verifyParamFunction: 2/2 parameter(s)
#>  PARAMETER      TABLECOLUMN   N   MAXABSDIFF   MAXRELDIFF PASS
#>         CL   CL / exp(ETA3) 748 0.0006296369 4.848771e-05 TRUE
#>       FREL FREL / exp(ETA2) 748 0.0001012091 5.217360e-05 TRUE

The value is a single TRUE/FALSE - TRUE only if every requested parameter was checked and passed - so it drops straight into if (verifyParamFunction(...)) .... The per-parameter table shown above is attached as attr(v, "checks").

Put both the parameters and the covariates in $TABLE. They then come from the same row of the same file and cannot be misaligned, and no $DATA filtering has to be reproduced to compare them. For run7, whose etaMap is

gen$etaMap
#> FREL   CL    V 
#>    2    3    4

a table carrying everything needed looks like this:

$TABLE ID TIME CL FREL V ETA2 ETA3 ETA4
       WT SEX FOOD FORM GENO1 GENO3 GENO4
       ONEHEADER NOPRINT FILE=xptab7

The parameters, the ETAs that carry their between-subject variability, and every covariate the parameter function reads. Three rules decide what happens for each parameter:

in the table what is used why
TVCL TVCL directly already a typical value, no ETA needed
CL and ETA3 CL / exp(ETA3) the tabled CL is the individual value; divide the IIV out
CL but no ETA3 nothing — warning, PASS = NA the individual value cannot be reduced to a typical one

If both CL and TVCL are present, TVCL wins. It is checked first and used as it stands, so the ETA column is not consulted at all. That is the cheaper and more direct comparison, and it does not depend on the parameter being written in the exponential-IIV form the etaMap recognises — so tabling TV-prefixed values is the more robust choice if you are adding columns specifically for this check.

If CL is tabled with no ETA3, that parameter is not checked. The function does not fall back to comparing the individual value against a typical one, which would fail for every subject with a non-zero ETA and tell you nothing. It warns, naming the column it wanted, and reports PASS = NA for that parameter — so the overall result is NA rather than TRUE, and a parameter that was never checked cannot be mistaken for one that passed.

The residual above is not error, it is the table’s precision: NONMEM’s default format carries about five significant digits, so agreement closer than roughly 1e-5 relative cannot be observed. tol defaults to 1e-4, just above that floor.

3. The reference row: dfRefRow

setupDfRefRow() builds the reference the other rows are expressed relative to. By default it computes the reference state from the data — mode for categorical, median or mean for continuous, on one record per subject — and maps it onto the geometry of a setupDfCovs() result.

It needs both dfCovs and covariates, which do different jobs. dfCovs gives the shape — the column names and their order, including the one-hot columns setupDfCovs() generated. covariates gives the base names to compute a reference for, the same vector passed to setupDfCovs(), in terms of the covariates as they exist in the data rather than after encoding:

covariates
#> [1] "WT"   "AGE"  "CRCL" "SEX"  "NCIL" "GENO"

So GENO appears in covariates once, and the resulting reference is written across the GENO_2, GENO_3, GENO_4 columns that dfCovs carries. Passing the encoded names instead would ask for a reference for each dummy separately, which is not the same question.

catRef and sep do not have to be repeated. They decide what the one-hot columns are called, and setupDfRefRow() has to agree with setupDfCovs() or the reference for those covariates is matched by a name that does not exist. Asking for the same two arguments twice and trusting they stay in step is a standing invitation to a silent mismatch, so setupDfCovs() records what it used on the object it returns and setupDfRefRow() reads it back:

str(attr(dfCovs, "pmxCovSetup"))
#> List of 5
#>  $ catRef         : NULL
#>  $ sep            : chr "_"
#>  $ missVal        : num -99
#>  $ covariates     : chr [1:6] "WT" "AGE" "CRCL" "SEX" ...
#>  $ conditionalCovs: NULL

Passing either argument explicitly still wins, which is what you want when dfCovs was built some other way. The record is an ordinary attribute, so subsetting dfCovs drops it — pass them by hand in that case, exactly as before.

covariates need not cover every column of dfCovs. It is the set of covariates you want a reference computed from the data for, not a description of dfCovs. Leave one out and its columns are set to missVal rather than to a data-derived value:

setupDfRefRow(dfCovs, data = dfData, covariates = c("WT", "AGE"), idVar = "ID")
#>     WT AGE CRCL SEX NCIL GENO_2 GENO_3 GENO_4 COVARIATEGROUPS
#> 1 85.4  47  -99 -99  -99    -99    -99    -99       Reference

That is a useful thing to be able to say, not a degraded result. missVal is what every parameter function already reads as “this covariate is not active here”, so it answers with its own reference — for a generated function, the one read out of $PK. So omitting a covariate here means use the model’s reference for this one and including it means use the data’s, which is a real choice and the same one Section 4 is about. A message names the columns so the choice is never made by accident.

singleRef = TRUE gives a one-row data frame with every covariate at its reference value:

setupDfRefRow(dfCovs, data = dfData, covariates = covariates, idVar = "ID")
#>     WT AGE CRCL SEX NCIL GENO_2 GENO_3 GENO_4 COVARIATEGROUPS
#> 1 85.4  47  118   1    0      1      0      0       Reference

singleRef = FALSE gives a data frame the same shape as dfCovs: active cells are replaced with the reference value, inactive cells keep -99. Use it when the reference should track the covariate that varies on each row.

head(setupDfRefRow(dfCovs,
  data = dfData, covariates = covariates,
  singleRef = FALSE, idVar = "ID"
), 4)
#>      WT AGE CRCL SEX NCIL GENO_2 GENO_3 GENO_4 COVARIATEGROUPS
#> 1  85.4 -99  -99 -99  -99    -99    -99    -99              WT
#> 2  85.4 -99  -99 -99  -99    -99    -99    -99              WT
#> 3 -99.0  47  -99 -99  -99    -99    -99    -99             AGE
#> 4 -99.0  47  -99 -99  -99    -99    -99    -99             AGE

contRef and catRef

These say how a reference value is chosen. Each takes either a single setting applied to every covariate, or a named list with an entry per covariate and an optional default component:

accepted values
contRef a number, "mean", "median" (default), "model"
catRef a level, "mode" (default), "lowest", "model" 
setupDfRefRow(dfCovs, dfData, covariates,
  idVar = "ID",
  contRef = list(WT = 75, default = "mean")
)
#>   WT  AGE CRCL SEX NCIL GENO_2 GENO_3 GENO_4 COVARIATEGROUPS
#> 1 75 45.9  117   1    0      1      0      0       Reference

contRef applies to setupDfCovs() too — to conditionalCovs, and to primary covariates when useMissVal = FALSE.

"model" needs the covariate to be in $PK

"model" reads the reference out of the control stream, by the same rules Section 2 lists. That makes it the setting that keeps the reference row and the parameter function consistent — Section 4 is about why that matters — but it only works for covariates $PK actually mentions.

As a bare scalar it applies to every covariate, so one unmentioned covariate fails the whole call. run7’s $PK never mentions AGE:

setupDfRefRow(dfCovs, dfData, covariates, idVar = "ID", contRef = "model", model = modFile)
#> Error: No reference value for covariate AGE could be derived from the model.
#> Give it explicitly, e.g. contRef = list(AGE = <value>).

Use the named-list form and let everything else fall back:

contRef = list(WT = "model", default = "median")

A one-hot coded categorical needs a literal level, not "model". $PK names the dummies GENO1, GENO3, GENO4 — never bare GENO — so the model holds a reference for each dummy but none for the covariate they encode:

catRef = list(GENO = "model")
#> Error: No reference value for covariate GENO could be derived from the model.
#> Give it explicitly, e.g. catRef = list(GENO = <level>).
#> The $PK names GENO4, GENO1, GENO3 rather than GENO itself, so a reference was
#> found for each of those but not for the covariate they encode. Give the level
#> you want as the reference.

So catRef = list(SEX = "model", FORM = "model", FOOD = "model", GENO = 2): SEX, FORM and FOOD are coded directly in $PK and resolve; GENO is given the level you want.

setupDfRefRow() keys the reference values by the column names setupDfCovs() produces. Pass it a dfCovs built by setupDfCovs(), and the same catRef and sep, so the columns line up. For a hand-built createInputForestData() structure, construct dfRefRow directly as a one-row data frame.

4. Keeping the reference and the parameter function consistent

This section is the reason the previous two sit in the same vignette.

A parameter function must return something when a covariate is inactive, and it falls back to the model’s own reference — the 75 in (WT/75), or the level in the branch marked ; Most common. If setupDfRefRow() meanwhile takes the median weight and the modal formulation from the data, the two disagree. Every row where that covariate is inactive is then displaced from 1, by a factor that looks entirely plausible on the plot.

For run7 the two disagree on both counts:

covsMod <- c("WT", "SEX", "FOOD", "FORM")
dfCovsM <- setupDfCovs(dfData, covariates = covsMod, idVar = "ID")

## From the data
setupDfRefRow(dfCovsM, dfData, covsMod, idVar = "ID")
#>     WT SEX FOOD FORM COVARIATEGROUPS
#> 1 85.4   1    1    0       Reference

## From the control stream
setupDfRefRow(dfCovsM, dfData, covsMod,
  idVar = "ID",
  contRef = "model", catRef = "model", model = modFile
)
#>   WT SEX FOOD FORM COVARIATEGROUPS
#> 1 75   1    1    1       Reference

WT is 85.4 in the data and 75 in the model; FORM is 0 in the data and 1 in the model. With the data-derived reference, every row that does not vary WT sits at (75/85.4)^theta instead of 1 — 0.907 for CL and 0.878 for V — and every row that does not vary FORM sits at 1.17 for Frel:

c(CL = (75 / 85.4)^thetas[2], V = (75 / 85.4)^thetas[3], Frel = 1 / (1 + thetas[12]))
#>        CL         V      Frel 
#> 0.9071990 0.8782201 1.1689727

Setting contRef = "model" and catRef = "model" removes the mismatch by construction. model takes either a control stream path or the list returned by createParamFunction(); passing the latter guarantees the reference row and the parameter function come from one derivation.

dfRefRow <- setupDfRefRow(dfCovsM, dfData, covsMod,
  idVar = "ID",
  contRef = "model", catRef = "model", model = gen
)
dfRefRow
#>   WT SEX FOOD FORM COVARIATEGROUPS
#> 1 75   1    1    1       Reference

inst/validation/compare-paramFunction.R in the installed package draws the two Forest plots side by side — a hand-written parameter function and a generated one — and reports the largest difference between them. It is a useful template for checking a translation on your own model.

5. Which records to summarise

Everything above summarises whatever data frame you hand it. NONMEM, meanwhile, reads only the records its $DATA IGNORE and ACCEPT statements leave, so what is in the data file and what the model was fitted to are not the same thing.

For users of pmxdata. This gives you the same record selection as pmxdata::analysis_data(), by a different route. analysis_data() reads the exclType specification and keeps the records where it is 0; filterByModel() replays the control stream’s own IGNORE/ACCEPT statements against a data frame you already have. In the standard workflow, where the model’s $DATA record is written to match the exclType specification, the two agree — and where they do not, the disagreement is worth understanding before going further, since one of them is not describing the model’s population.

PMXForest is a public package and deliberately does not depend on pmxdata, which is internal; if you have pmxdata available, either route is fine.

dfUsed <- filterByModel(dfData, modFile, quiet = TRUE)

c(
  records_file = nrow(dfData), records_model = nrow(dfUsed),
  subjects_file = length(unique(dfData$ID)),
  subjects_model = length(unique(dfUsed$ID))
)
#>   records_file  records_model  subjects_file subjects_model 
#>          69016          33885            964            754

Over a fifth of the subjects in the file were never seen by run7, and that moves the quantiles the plot is built from:

getCovStats(dfData, "CRCL", idVar = "ID")
#> $CRCL
#>    5%   95% 
#>  74.9 150.0
getCovStats(dfUsed, "CRCL", idVar = "ID")
#> $CRCL
#>    5%   95% 
#>  77.7 150.0

So summarise filterByModel(dfData, modFile) rather than the raw file — or pass a $TABLE output, which is already filtered.

filterByModel() matches columns by position, not by name. NONMEM skips the header line and takes its names from $INPUT, so the two can disagree — and in this very data set they do:

mod <- PMXForest:::nmReadModel(modFile)
data.frame(
  position = 9:10,
  input = PMXForest:::nmInputPositions(mod)$names[9:10],
  csv_header = names(dfData)[9:10]
)
#>   position input csv_header
#> 1        9   ODV         DV
#> 2       10    DV       LNDV

$INPUT’s DV is the file’s LNDV. Filtering by name would read the wrong column. useInputNames = TRUE returns the data as NONMEM sees it, renamed.

The single-character form (IGNORE=C) is a rule about the first character of each raw record rather than a condition on the data, so it cannot be applied to a data frame; it is skipped with a warning. The conventional @ and # header markers are skipped silently, since read.csv() has already dealt with them.

6. Parameter uncertainty: dfParameters

getSamples() builds the sampled parameter vectors, from a .cov file (a multivariate normal draw around the estimates), a PsN bootstrap, a SIR raw_results file, or a data frame you supply.

dfSamples <- getSamples(
  system.file("extdata", "SimVal/run7.cov", package = "PMXForest"),
  system.file("extdata", "SimVal/run7.ext", package = "PMXForest"),
  n = 25
)
dim(dfSamples)
#> [1] 26 31

The first row is always the final estimates, so row 1 of the Forest plot data is the point estimate and the remaining rows give the interval. noBaseThetas says how many leading columns to pass to the parameter function; createParamFunction() reports the right value for the model it read.

gen$noBaseThetas
#> [1] 14

See the Walkthrough for the full treatment, including bootstrap and SIR inputs.

7. Empirical Forest plots: covExpressionsList

getForestDFemp() takes a named list of expression() objects, one per Forest plot row, each selecting the subjects it summarises. setupCovExpressionsList() builds that list — and the matching cdfCovsNames labels — from the same deduplicated statistics setupDfCovs() uses.

emp <- setupCovExpressionsList(
  data       = dfUsed,
  covariates = c("WT", "SEX", "GENO"),
  idVar      = "ID"
)
emp$covExpressionsList
#> $WT
#> expression(WT < 58.3)
#> 
#> $WT
#> expression(WT >= 126)
#> 
#> $SEX
#> expression(SEX == 1)
#> 
#> $SEX
#> expression(SEX == 2)
#> 
#> $GENO
#> expression(GENO == 1)
#> 
#> $GENO
#> expression(GENO == 2)
#> 
#> $GENO
#> expression(GENO == 3)
#> 
#> $GENO
#> expression(GENO == 4)
emp$cdfCovsNames
#> [1] "WT <58.3" "WT >=126" "SEX 1"    "SEX 2"    "GENO 1"   "GENO 2"   "GENO 3"  
#> [8] "GENO 4"

Continuous covariates become two rows at the probs quantile tails (WT < q_05, WT >= q_95); contSplit = "median" splits at the median instead so every subject falls in one row. Binary and multi-level categorical covariates become one == level row per level; includeReference = FALSE drops the reference level, as in the parametric dfCovs.

An conditionalCovs entry gets its own rows and contributes a fixed condition that is combined with & into every other covariate’s expression: a level for a categorical covariate, or a prob / value split with a direction for a continuous one. Use it to restrict the empirical contrast to a sub-population.

setupCovExpressionsList(
  data = dfUsed,
  covariates = c("WT", "SEX"),
  contSplit = "median",
  conditionalCovs = list(FOOD = 1, CRCL = list(prob = 0.25, dir = "gt")),
  idVar = "ID"
)$covExpressionsList
#> $WT
#> expression(WT < 83.9 & FOOD == 1 & CRCL > 99.3)
#> 
#> $WT
#> expression(WT >= 83.9 & FOOD == 1 & CRCL > 99.3)
#> 
#> $SEX
#> expression(SEX == 1 & FOOD == 1 & CRCL > 99.3)
#> 
#> $SEX
#> expression(SEX == 2 & FOOD == 1 & CRCL > 99.3)
#> 
#> $FOOD
#> expression(FOOD == 0 & CRCL > 99.3)
#> 
#> $FOOD
#> expression(FOOD == 1 & CRCL > 99.3)
#> 
#> $CRCL
#> expression(CRCL < 119 & FOOD == 1)
#> 
#> $CRCL
#> expression(CRCL >= 119 & FOOD == 1)

Every generated expression is evaluated against the deduplicated data. If any selects fewer than minSubjects subjects (default 10) the function stops, so an empty or near-empty subset never reaches getForestDFemp().

setupCovExpressionsList(dfUsed, "WT", probs = c(0.001, 0.999), idVar = "ID")
#> Error in setupCovExpressionsList(dfUsed, "WT", probs = c(0.001, 0.999), : Expression `WT < 46.7` selects 1 subject(s) in `data`, fewer than `minSubjects` (10). Relax `minSubjects`, widen `probs`, or adjust the split / `conditionalCovs` conditions.

The reference for an empirical plot stays deterministic: build it with setupDfCovs() and setupDfRefRow(singleRef = TRUE) and pass the one-row data frame to getForestDFemp(dfRefRow = ), exactly as for a parametric plot.

8. Missing covariate values

getCovStats() and the setup functions exclude missVal before computing statistics, so a covariate that is missing for some subjects is summarised from the subjects who have it.

dfMiss <- data.frame(
  ID  = 1:8,
  WT  = c(60.5, 70.2, 70.5, 80.8, 65.1, 90.0, 77.4, 68.9),
  SEX = c(0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0),
  BMI = c(22.1, 24.4, -99, 27.3, 23.5, 28.9, -99, 25.1)
)

getCovStats(dfMiss, c("WT", "SEX", "BMI"), idVar = "ID", minLevels = 4)
#> $WT
#>   5%  95% 
#> 62.1 86.8 
#> 
#> $SEX
#> [1] 0 1
#> 
#> $BMI
#>   5%  95% 
#> 22.5 28.5

The BMI quantiles are computed from the six non-missing values. The parameter function still has to handle -99 in the BMI column of dfCovs, because that is what marks the rows where BMI is inactive — which is exactly what the preamble in Section 2 does.

9. Feeding the result forward

Putting the four inputs together:

dfUsed    <- filterByModel(dfData, modFile)
dfCovs    <- setupDfCovs(dfUsed, covariates = covs, idVar = "ID")
gen       <- createParamFunction(modFile, parameters = c("CL", "V"))
paramFunc <- eval(parse(text = gen$code))          # after reading it
dfRefRow  <- setupDfRefRow(dfCovs, dfUsed, covs, idVar = "ID",
                           contRef = "model", catRef = "model", model = gen)
dfSamples <- getSamples(covFile, extFile, n = 1000)

dfres <- getForestDFSCM(
  dfCovs           = dfCovs,
  functionList     = list(paramFunc),
  functionListName = gen$functionListName,
  noBaseThetas     = gen$noBaseThetas,
  dfParameters     = dfSamples,
  dfRefRow         = dfRefRow
)

See the Walkthrough for the full call and the plotting step.

For empirical Forest plots, getForestDFemp() takes covExpressionsList in place of dfCovs. If the parameter function is written against one-hot dummy columns (GENO_2, GENO_3, …) rather than the raw GENO, give getForestDFemp() its own oneHot argument — the same spec oneHotEncode() takes — so those columns are added to the data passed in before the parameter function runs. The expressions from setupCovExpressionsList() always filter on the raw column, so that choice is independent of how the expression list is built.
